comment: Alert rules over the production metrics, not over the application (EV-29).
Each rule carries two labels that form the contract between Grafana and the Conflict
Sentinel. stripboardTrigger says which kind of disruption to open. stripboardAction
says what to do about it, and the distinction turned out to matter: a rule about the
schedule's quality blocks no scene, so there is nothing for the replanner to absorb.
replan       something happened — re-solve around the blocked scene-dates
consolidate  nothing happened; the plan is poor — re-solve under a tighter cap and
report what obeying it costs
A rule without a stripboardTrigger is one nobody can act on, so the provisioner refuses
to create it. stripboardAction defaults to replan when absent.
Thresholds are deliberately conservative. An alert that fires constantly is one a 1st
AD learns to ignore, and an alerting system nobody reads is worse than none.
They are also calibrated against schedules this solver actually produces, not guessed.
shoot_risk_index is deliberately NOT alerted on, and that is a finding rather than an
omission. The first draft set it at 60; no real schedule came close, including ones the
project itself considers poor — the 14-scene demo scores 44 while running a day that
visits four locations. Lowering the threshold to 45 would have made it fire on that
schedule and taught us nothing, because a composite index cannot say what to do about
itself. It stays on the dashboard, where a number that means 'this shoot is tight' is
worth reading. Every rule below names a specific, fixable condition instead.

rules.title: Unit hopping between locations in a day
rules.summary: At least one shooting day visits more than two locations. Each company move costs about an hour of shooting light, so a day with three or more is a day largely spent in the van.
rules.runbook: Re-solve with a cap of two locations per day and read what it costs in shooting days. Nothing is blocked here, so there is no disruption to absorb — only a trade to price.

rules.title: Union violation in the committed schedule
rules.summary: The committed schedule breaks a union rule. This is a legal exposure, not a preference: it must be replanned before the call sheets go out.
rules.runbook: Open Proposals & Approval and re-solve. UnionRulesService names the rule that was broken.

rules.title: Cast paid to wait
rules.summary: At least one cast member is called on under a third of shooting days. That is a contract being paid against days not worked — the exact waste a Day Out of Days schedule exists to prevent.
rules.runbook: Group that actor's scenes into consecutive days, even at the cost of a company move.
rules.note: A ratio threshold interacts with the length of the shoot: on a two-day schedule the lowest possible non-zero utilisation is 0.5, so this cannot fire. That is intended — a two-day shoot has no idle-cast problem worth waking anyone for. It bites from four days upward, which is where the waste becomes real money.

rules.title: Schedule cost above budget
rules.summary: The committed schedule now costs more than the budget line. The figure is the solver's estimate: crew and called cast per day, plus move and penalty costs.
rules.runbook: Compare against the previous committed version in the Audit Trail to see which change added the cost.
